statement: The goal of test-driven development is clean code that works, delivered now.
Write new production code only when an automated test is currently failing.
Continuously eliminate duplication in the code as the second core rule of TDD.
The TDD cycle has three phases in fixed order: red, then green, then refactor.
In the red phase, write a small test that does not yet work and may not even compile.
In the green phase, make the failing test pass as quickly as possible, even with ugly or expedient code.
In the refactor phase, remove all duplication introduced while getting the test to pass.
The TDD working rhythm is: add a test, run all tests and watch the new one fail, make a small change, run all tests and see them pass, then refactor to remove duplication.
The harder the programming problem, the smaller the increment of functionality each test should cover.
condition: the programming problem is difficult

statement: Each test should cover only a small increment of functionality.
Run the automated tests frequently, after each small change.
TDD is a technique for managing fear during programming by closing the gap between decision and feedback.
Designs should consist of many highly cohesive, loosely coupled components so that testing is easy.
The development environment must provide rapid response to small changes for TDD to be practical.
Developers should write their own tests rather than waiting for someone else to write them.
Grow the design organically, letting running code provide feedback between design decisions.
Some software cannot be driven solely by tests, such as security software and subtle concurrency problems.
exception: the goals depend on human judgment or cannot be reliably reproduced by running code, as with security and concurrency

statement: Start from a test rather than from objects or code.
When writing a test, imagine the perfect interface for the operation and work backward from that ideal API.
Begin with the simplest test you can make pass: start small or not at all.
Keep a to-do list of tests to write; mark an item in progress, cross it off when done, and add new tests as they occur to you.
When a test will not compile, do the least work needed to make it compile, fixing one compile error at a time.
Seek a concrete numerical measure of progress, such as the count of remaining compile errors or failing tests.
Reducing defect density far enough lets quality assurance shift from reactive to proactive work.
condition: defect density is reduced sufficiently

statement: A failing (red) test is concrete progress: it converts a vague problem into a specific, smaller, testable one.
During the green phase the goal is only to pass the test, not to produce the perfect or final answer.
A limited or naive implementation that passes the test is not enough; generalize the code before moving to the next test.
Dependency is the key problem in software development at all scales.
Duplication is the visible symptom whose underlying problem is dependency.
Eliminating duplication in code eliminates dependency, unlike most cases where removing a symptom just moves the problem.
Remove duplication before writing the next test so the next test can be made to pass with a single change.
Duplication can exist between the data in the test and the data in the code, not only between two pieces of code.
TDD is not about always taking tiny steps; it is about being able to take tiny steps when the problem gets hard.
Getting the bar green quickly excuses any expedient sins, but only momentarily; afterward you must make the code right.
Solve 'make it work' first and 'make it clean' second, the opposite of architecture-driven development.
A Value Object's instance-variable values must never change after they are set in the constructor.
Every operation on a Value Object must return a new object rather than mutating the receiver.
Value Objects eliminate aliasing bugs because a shared value can never be mutated underneath another reference.
A Value Object should implement equals() since one instance of a given value is as good as another.
If a Value Object is used as a hash-table key and implements equals(), it must also implement hashCode().
condition: the object is used as a key in a hash table and implements equals()

statement: Translate a design objection or aesthetic discomfort (such as unwanted side effects) into a concrete failing test case.
Fake It is a get-to-green strategy: return a constant, then gradually replace constants with variables until the code is real.
Obvious Implementation is a get-to-green strategy: type in the real implementation directly when it is clear and quick.
condition: the clean simple solution is obvious and fast to type

statement: Shift to Obvious Implementation when confident, and fall back to Fake It plus refactoring as soon as you get an unexpected red bar.
Triangulation generalizes code only once two or more concrete examples demand the more general solution.
condition: two or more examples are present

statement: Use Triangulation only when you are unsure how to refactor; otherwise remove the duplication and generalize directly.
exception: you can already see how to eliminate the duplication and write the general solution

statement: Defer operations that are not needed yet (such as null comparison or hashCode) by adding them to the to-do list instead of implementing them now.
Make an instance variable private as soon as comparing objects directly removes the need for outside access to it.
Expressing each behavior twice, as code and as a test, reduces defects but does not guarantee correctness when two related tests fail together.
Do not strive for perfection: accept that some defects will slip through, learn the test you should have written, and move on.
When a test is too big to implement in one step, invent a smaller test that represents real progress toward it.
Copying and editing existing code to reach green quickly is acceptable, provided the duplication is removed before the next test.
exception: the duplication is left in place past the refactor step

statement: Introduce factory methods so tests and client code do not depend on concrete subclasses, freeing you to change the inheritance structure without touching model code.
Reconcile two near-duplicate methods by having them return a common supertype as a first step toward merging them.
Eliminate duplication by moving identical declarations, variables, and constructors up into a common superclass.
Make constructors identical by pushing their variation out to the caller (such as a factory method) so the constructor body can be shared.
Before deleting a test, ask whether removing it would lose any confidence in the code; keep it if it still exercises unique logic, and treat a fully redundant test as a deletion candidate.
condition: the test still exercises logic not covered elsewhere

statement: Entertain only a brief interruption to a refactoring, and never interrupt an interruption.
exception: the interruption itself gets interrupted by yet another task

statement: When a larger step produces a mistake, unwind the changes, shift to smaller steps, and redo the work.
TDD is a steering process: continuously adjust step size, taking bigger steps when confident and smaller steps when unsure, because there is no single right step size.
Rather than spend minutes reasoning about whether a change is safe, make the change and run the tests to let the computer answer faster.
condition: you have tests that give you confidence in the code

statement: Improve a confusing test-failure message by adding diagnostics such as a toString() implementation.
You cannot change real model code without a supporting test.
Writing a little code without a test first is an acceptable exception when the result will be seen immediately, the risk is low (such as debug-only output), or you already have a red bar.
exception: the result is about to be shown on screen, the failure risk is low, or a red bar is already present

statement: The conservative response to a red bar before changing model code is to back out the change to return to green, then write the test, fix the code, and reapply the change.
Equality should compare the meaningful attributes of an object (such as its currency), not its concrete class.
Prefer not to write a new test while a red bar is showing.
Choose test parameters that deliberately break the current implementation so the test forces a real change.
Write ugly code with casts in one place to reach a green bar, then move the code where it belongs once the tests pass.
Do not add a parameter or capability speculatively because you think you will need it later; add it when a test demands it.
exception: a current test actually requires it

statement: Whenever you find yourself checking an object's class explicitly, replace the class check with polymorphism.
Promote a shared method onto a common interface so polymorphic dispatch eliminates casts and explicit class checks.
Do not mark a test as done until the duplication it introduced has been eliminated.
Write a small test to verify an assumption about how the programming language or library behaves before relying on it.
Within a refactoring you may add a private helper class without its own separate tests, relying on existing tests to exercise it.
exception: the helper's logic becomes complex or a collaborator cannot see where the refactoring is going, in which case write separate tests

statement: Use a quick, deliberately suboptimal implementation to get running fast, and improve it later with real usage data.
condition: a faster correct-enough implementation lets you keep moving

statement: Follow the compiler: treat its compile errors as a to-do list that ripples changes and keeps you focused.
When generalizing types, change declarations from the leaves and edges back toward the root test case to avoid a cascading ripple of breakage.
When a desired test cannot be made to compile or pass quickly, back off to a more specific achievable test, get to green, then generalize.
When a surprising red bar reveals something you did not expect, write a test that captures and communicates the discovery.
After a mistake in a refactoring you may forge ahead and write another test to isolate the problem instead of backing the change out.
Separate two intertwined responsibilities so each can be worked on independently, recombining them later only if that proves right.
Generalize code that works for one instance into code that works for many by replacing constants with variables.
TDD makes generalization reliable by giving you concrete running examples to generalize from instead of reasoning in the abstract.
Place operations near the data they act on, moving a method to the class that owns the attributes it uses.
Run the tests between every refactoring step to confirm the behavior is unchanged.
It is not necessary to always work in tiny steps; mastery of TDD is being able to take tiny steps when the situation calls for them.
Avoid Pluggable Selector because it makes code hard to analyze statically.
Most tests follow the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern: create objects, stimulate them, then check the results.
Test performance (sharing objects across tests) and test isolation (each test independent of others) are competing constraints that must be balanced.
Avoid test coupling: shared mutable state makes one broken test cascade failures and lets test-ordering hide real bugs.
Run each test in a fresh instance with freshly created objects so that tests cannot couple through shared state.
exception: the objects interact through global variables or other hidden shared state

statement: Use a setUp() method to build a clean fixture before each test, favoring simplicity of test writing over raw performance.
A test may be simplified to stop checking something only if another test reliably covers that behavior.
condition: another test already verifies the dropped behavior

statement: Use a tearDown() method to release external resources allocated in setUp() so tests stay independent.
condition: a test allocates external resources

statement: Record method calls in an ordered log rather than many boolean flags to assert both that methods ran and the order in which they ran.
When building a testing framework, focus on supporting a set of isolated, composable test cases rather than on implementation details.
Distinguish assertion failures from other errors in a test runner, presenting them separately, because assertion failures take much longer to debug.
Implementing xUnit yourself in a new language is a fast way to explore the language facilities you will use in daily programming.
Having tests (an automated procedure that accepts or rejects) is fundamentally different from manually testing a change by poking buttons and reading the screen.
Stress and testing form a vicious loop: more stress leads to less testing, more errors, and still more stress; automated testing inverts it into a virtuous cycle.
Running a new test even when you expect it to fail can surface a mistaken assumption, so it is sometimes worth running.
Tests should not affect one another at all: one broken test should mean exactly one problem.
Make tests fast enough that you run them yourself and run them often, catching errors before anyone else sees them.
Seek tests at a smaller scale than the whole application so a single failure does not leave the system in an unpredictable state for later tests.
Isolated tests are order independent, so any subset can be run without a prerequisite test breaking it.
Isolating tests forces you to compose the system from many highly cohesive, loosely coupled objects.
Before you begin coding, write a list of all the tests you know you will need.
Do not take a step forward in a programming session unless you know where your foot will land.
Write the to-do list down rather than holding it in your head, which drains attention and reduces what you accomplish.
Populate the test list with an example of every operation to implement, a null or degenerate version of operations that do not yet exist, and the refactorings needed for clean code.
Do not implement all tests at once: each implemented test adds inertia against refactoring, and many broken tests keep you far from green.
exception: automated refactoring tools reduce the inertia of many existing tests

statement: In pure TDD you are never more than one change away from a green bar, like the climbing rule of keeping three of four limbs attached.
As tests pass, the implementation will imply new tests and refactorings; write them on the list rather than acting immediately.
Handle every item left on the list at session end: defer out-of-scope refactorings to a later list, but never defer a test you suspect might fail.
exception: a pending test might not pass, in which case getting it to work outranks releasing

statement: Write the test before you write the code it tests.
Test-first is primarily a design and scope-control tool, not merely after-the-fact verification.
Write a test's assertions first, then work backward to create the objects and setup the assertions require.
Start a system from the stories you want to tell about it, start a feature from the tests it should pass, and start a test from the asserts that should pass when it is done.
Asserting first separates the questions 'what is the right answer?' and 'how will I check it?' from the other problems a test poses.
Use test data that makes the test easy to read, and make any difference between data values meaningful rather than arbitrary.
Reflect multiple inputs in tests when the system must handle multiple inputs, but use no more data than is needed to drive the same design decisions.
condition: the system must handle multiple inputs

statement: Never use the same constant to mean more than one thing in a test; choose distinct values so a reversed-argument bug cannot hide.
Prefer Realistic Data over made-up data when testing against real-time event traces, doing parallel testing against a prior system, or refactoring a simulation that must produce identical answers.
condition: testing real-time traces, parallel testing, or refactoring a simulation expecting identical results

statement: Include both expected and actual results in the test and make their relationship apparent, because you are writing the test for a future human reader.
Pick the next test as one that will teach you something and that you are confident you can implement.
Programs grown from tests develop from the known toward the unknown rather than strictly top-down or bottom-up.
Start with a degenerate Starter Test whose output equals its input and whose input is as small as possible, so you only have to answer where the operation belongs.
Keep the red-green-refactor loop down to minutes by choosing inputs and outputs that are trivially easy to discover.
Spread TDD by asking for and giving explanations in terms of concrete test cases, never by forcing the practice on people.
Before using a new external library facility for the first time, write a Learning Test that verifies the API behaves as you expect, and re-run those tests when new releases arrive.
condition: you are about to use an unfamiliar third-party API

statement: When a tangential idea arises during a technical discussion, add a test to the list and return to the topic.
On a defect report, first write the smallest possible failing test that the fix will repair, then ask how you could have known to write it originally.
condition: a defect has been reported

statement: When you feel lost and the code has become a mess, throw the code away and start over rather than trying to untwist it.
condition: you are lost and cannot see how to proceed

statement: Switching pair-programming partners is an effective way to motivate productive do-overs, since a fresh partner is uninvested in the existing mess.
Allocate hardware and furniture deliberately: buy the best chairs and the fastest shared development machines, economizing on individual machines and other furniture.
When a test turns out to be too big, write a smaller child test for the broken part, get it running, then reintroduce the larger test.
condition: a test requires several changes at once to pass

statement: Maintaining the red-green-refactor rhythm is worth extra effort; minimize the time spent sitting at a red bar.
When a test was too big, pause to learn why and what would have made it smaller before deleting and restarting it.
To test an object that depends on an expensive or complicated resource, create a fake version of the resource that returns constants.
condition: the real resource is slow, fragile, or hard to set up

statement: Mock objects improve not just test performance and reliability but also readability, since expected interactions are visible in the test.
Mock objects push you to consider the visibility of every object and to avoid storing expensive resources in globals or Singletons, reducing coupling.
Mock objects add the risk that the fake does not behave like the real object; mitigate it with a shared test set that runs against both the mock and the real object.
exception: the mock diverges in behavior from the real object

statement: To test that one object communicates correctly with another, have the object under test communicate with the test case itself (Self Shunt).
Self Shunt tests read better because the expected and actual values sit together in one place.
Keep interfaces as narrow as possible, and have empty stub implementations either return a reasonable value or throw, depending on whether an unexpected call should be flagged.
To test the order in which messages are called, append to a string log as each message runs; use a set comparison instead when order does not matter.
To test error-handling code that is rarely invoked, invoke it deliberately with a special object that throws an exception instead of doing real work.
Code that is not tested does not work, so test an error condition only if you want it to work.
Override just the single method needed (for example via an anonymous inner class) to simulate an error, keeping the test readable.
When programming alone, end a session by leaving the last test broken as a concrete bookmark for where to resume.
condition: you are working solo

statement: When programming on a team, end a session with all tests passing.
condition: you share the codebase with teammates

statement: Always make sure every test passes before you check in code.
Never comment out a test to make the suite pass.
When an integration test breaks on check-in, either discard your work and start over or allow yourself a few minutes to fix it before starting over.
condition: a test fails in the integration suite at check-in time

statement: Run the whole test suite all the time until it becomes annoyingly slow.
The first implementation after a broken test can be to return a constant, then gradually transform it into a real expression using variables (Fake It).
Having something running and green is better than having nothing running, especially when tests prove it works.
A green bar provides psychological certainty and scope control by letting you generalize from one concrete example instead of imagining future problems.
Drive abstraction conservatively by triangulating: introduce the general solution only once you have two or more examples.
condition: you are unsure of the correct abstraction

statement: Use Triangulation only when you are very unsure of the correct abstraction; otherwise use Obvious Implementation or Fake It.
exception: you already know the correct abstraction

statement: When you are sure how to implement a simple operation quickly, just type in the obvious implementation.
condition: the implementation is simple and you are confident

statement: Relying solely on Obvious Implementation demands perfection and is psychologically risky; downshift to smaller steps when red bars start surprising you.
Implement an operation for a single object first, then extend it to work with collections (One to Many).
Isolate a change by adding a parameter in the test so the implementation can change without affecting the test, and vice versa.
Automate result-checking with boolean assertions so that no human judgment remains in evaluating whether the code worked.
Make assertions specific (assert the area equals 50, not merely that it is non-zero), and put the expected value first in equality assertions for informative failure messages.
Avoid assertions that depend on the current implementation, such as an object's concrete class; assert observable behavior so the test survives a representation change.
Factor common fixture setup into setUp() when readers cannot easily remember the fixture, but keep setup inline when top-to-bottom readability matters more.
condition: readers cannot easily remember the fixture objects

statement: Make each distinct kind of fixture its own TestCase subclass; each fixture is created in an instance, used once, then discarded.
There is no simple one-to-one mapping between test classes and model classes.
Release external resources in tearDown(), because the goal of each test is to leave the world in exactly the same state as before it ran.
condition: a test acquires external resources

statement: Represent a single test case as a method whose name begins with 'test', and make the rest of the name explain to a future reader why the test exists.
Keep test methods short, readable, straight-line code, and take smaller steps when a test method grows long and complicated.
Outline the categories of tests you intend to write, then fill in specific tests under each; the outline becomes documentation of the class's contract.
Test an expected exception by catching exactly that exception and ignoring it, calling fail() if the exception is not thrown.
Run all tests together by composing a suite of suites: one per package and one aggregating them for the whole application.
Most programming problems are generated by the tools we use rather than by the external problem, so common internal subproblems recur with common solutions.
Design in TDD treats refactoring as a design activity, not as a separate up-front design phase.
Use the Command pattern when a plain message is not enough: represent the invocation of a computation as an object seeded with its parameters and triggered through generic protocol such as run().
condition: invocation must be more manipulable than a simple method call

statement: Design a Value Object by setting its state at creation and never changing it, with every operation returning a new object; use it when identity is unimportant and the object is widely shared.
The aliasing problem: when two objects share a reference to a third and one mutates it, the other can no longer rely on the shared object's state.
Every Value Object must implement equality, and in many languages must therefore also implement hashing.
Address Value Object allocation performance only when you have realistic data, realistic usage patterns, profiling data, and actual complaints.
condition: performance complaints are backed by profiling on realistic workloads

statement: Use a Null Object to represent a special or base case as an object with the same protocol as regular objects, eliminating repeated null checks.
Use a Template Method written entirely in terms of other methods to express an invariant computation sequence while allowing subclasses to refine the steps.
Declare a Template Method substep abstract (or raise a subclass-responsibility error) when the computation makes no sense without that substep being supplied.
condition: the computation is meaningless without the substep

statement: Discover Template Methods through experience and refactoring by extracting the variant parts, rather than designing them up front, then move the template to the superclass to remove duplication.
Replace a spreading explicit conditional with a Pluggable Object that has two or more implementations, acting the second time you see the conditional.
condition: the same conditional distinction appears more than once

statement: Use a Pluggable Selector to store a method name and invoke it dynamically, avoiding many subclasses that each implement a single method.
condition: each of several subclasses implements only one method in a straightforward situation

statement: The main drawback of Pluggable Selector is the difficulty of tracing whether a method is invoked, so it can be overused.

Use a Factory Method to create an object through a method instead of a constructor when you need the flexibility to return a different class without changing callers; otherwise plain constructors are fine.
exception: you do not need creation flexibility, in which case a constructor suffices

statement: Introduce variation by adding a new implementation of an existing protocol (an Imposter) rather than by adding conditional logic.
Add an if-statement only when there is an obvious single place for it and it does not duplicate logic elsewhere; otherwise use polymorphism.
exception: the variation would require changes across several methods

statement: Implement an object whose behavior composes a list of other objects by making it a Composite that imposts for its components through a shared interface.
Composite often introduces a conceptual disconnect from the real world, but the simplification it gives the code is usually worth that disconnect.
Discovering Imposters and Composites during refactoring is driven by eliminating duplication, like all refactoring.
Collect results of an operation spread across several objects by passing a Collecting Parameter into which each object accumulates its result.
A Collecting Parameter is a common consequence of Composite and is introduced as the sophistication of expected results grows.
Do not introduce global variables (Singletons) to languages that lack them; invest the time in better design instead.
In TDD a refactoring preserves the semantics that matter, namely the currently passing tests, which obliges you to have enough tests for that equivalence to be trustworthy.
That all tests passed is no excuse to check in code you know is flawed; write more tests instead.
Unify two similar pieces of code by gradually bringing them closer and merging them only when they are absolutely identical.
Avoid leap-of-faith refactorings that rely on long chains of reasoning; reduce their incidence with small steps and concrete feedback.
Reconciling differences applies at every scale: make two loops, conditional branches, methods, or classes identical so one can be merged or eliminated.
Sometimes reconcile differences backward by arranging for the last step of the change to be trivial, then working backward to it.
Isolate the part of a method or object that must change before changing it, like surgical draping, so you can focus on a fixed set of variables.
After isolating and making a trivial change, consider inlining to undo the isolation, balancing the cost of an extra method against the value of making a concept explicit.
Migrate between data representations by temporarily duplicating the data: add the new format, set and use it everywhere the old one was, then delete the old format.
Use Extract Method to turn a small part of a long method into its own well-named method, improving readability and removing duplication.
Use Inline Method to replace a call with the method body when control flow has become too twisted, and to reel yourself back from over-abstraction.
Introduce a second implementation in a typed language with Extract Interface, naming the interface for the underlying concept rather than prefixing it with 'I'.
Treat more than one message sent to another object within a method as a signal to apply Move Method and relocate that logic to the object it belongs to.
condition: a method sends several messages to the same other object

statement: Move Method is valuable because the need is visible without deep understanding, its mechanics are quick and safe, and its results are often enlightening.
Turn a complicated method with many parameters and locals into a Method Object so its locals become instance variables and you gain a namespace for further extraction.
condition: a method's many temporaries and parameters resist Extract Method

statement: Add a parameter by adding it to any interface first, then using compiler errors to find every caller that must change.

Keep a redundant test if removing it would reduce confidence in the system or if it communicates a distinct scenario to a reader; delete the less useful one only when it is redundant on both confidence and communication.
condition: two tests are redundant for both confidence and communication

statement: In languages and environments where the test-compile-run-refactor cycle is slow, you will be tempted to take larger steps and refactor with fewer intermediate steps.
TDD's effectiveness is independent of system size, because eliminating duplication yields many small objects that can be tested in isolation regardless of the application's scale.

Driving development only with small-scale unit tests risks building what you think users want rather than what they actually want; application-level tests let users specify exactly what the system should do next.

Application-level TDD faces a technical fixturing problem (testing features that do not exist yet) and a social problem (users writing tests before implementation), which organizations tend to resist.
Do not combine learning red-green-refactor with application fixturing and organizational change at once; establish red-green-refactor in your own practice first, then spread it.
Keep programmer-level TDD even when using application tests, to get immediate green bars and a simpler internal design.
When adopting TDD on an existing codebase, do not try to test and refactor the whole system at once, since that yields months with no new functionality.
condition: you are introducing TDD into a large legacy codebase

statement: Limit the scope of changes when adopting TDD midstream: leave working but ugly parts that do not currently need to change alone.

Break the deadlock between tests and refactoring on legacy code using other feedback, such as working carefully with a partner and using imperfect system-level tests, to make the code more accepting of change.
TDD encodes a value system that assumes writing better code leads to more success, so it is not for those who slam code together and never revisit it.
Good engineering is roughly twenty percent of a project's success: bad engineering can sink a project, but modest engineering can enable success when the other eighty percent lines up.
Reducing repeatable behavior to explicit rules makes applying them rote and fast, freeing time and energy for creativity when a genuine exception arises.
When using TDD to implement a pattern-driven design, think about what you want the system to do and let the design emerge, because pre-committed design ideas often turn out wrong.
The sooner a defect is found and fixed, the cheaper it is, often dramatically so.
There is no scientific proof that TDD beats its alternatives in quality, productivity, or enjoyment; the supporting evidence is anecdotal.
TDD shortens the feedback loop on design decisions, turning an idea into a concrete test or interface within seconds or minutes instead of weeks.
Writing a test for every feature, refactoring between steps, and adding features one at a time only after all tests pass makes the code behave like an attractor that converges toward correctness.
TDD is fundamentally an analysis and design technique for structuring all development activities, not merely a testing technique.
Drive development with tests rather than with speculation or specifications.
Pairing complements TDD: the tests are shared conversation pieces and a fresh partner can take over when TDD's rhythm leads you to keep working while tired.
Work when you are fresh and stop when you are tired; take a break when you cannot get a test, or two tests together, to work.
A passing test plus removed duplication is a natural point to integrate, letting TDD shorten continuous-integration cycles to roughly 15 to 30 minutes.
Achieve simple design by coding only what the tests need and removing all duplication, yielding a design adapted to current requirements.
Higher confidence from a growing test suite lets you attempt more aggressive large-scale refactorings that extend the system's life.
Focus on one mode at a time: while adding functionality only try to get a test to pass, and while refactoring only try to get the design right.
TDD produces a 'rapid unhurriedness' in which steady, unhurried, one-ball-at-a-time progress turns out to be fast.
When reusing a pattern, copy it fairly blindly first and then adapt it with refactoring or test-first, since patterns are half-baked and must be adapted to your project.
Break programming into elemental modes such as test-first, refactoring, and pattern-copying, and switch rapidly between them to gain focus without monotony.
Choose a system of development practices that support one another so you do about the right amount of each activity even under stress.

Design practice systems by creating virtuous cycles for good activities, avoiding death spirals that grow destructive activities, and adding negative feedback loops to prevent overuse of good activities.

Repair a misbehaving practice system by driving a positive loop the other direction (for example, making more tests pass to rebuild confidence), introducing a negative feedback loop to curb an overgrown activity, or breaking connections that form unhelpful loops.
Drive a test from a table of input and expected-output values to factor out duplicated assertion structure and make adding cases cheap.
Combine related assertions in a single test method when splitting them into separate methods adds no communication value.
exception: separate methods would communicate distinct scenarios to a reader

statement: Generalize a literal by rewriting it as the expression it actually represents, then replacing the parts with the real computation.
